nameStory: The 'contracta' part of this clam's name comes from the Latin word meaning 'drawn together' or 'contracted,' referring to how tightly the two shell halves can clamp shut. Like a tiny underwater vault, this little clam can seal itself up so securely that it's nearly impossible to pry open when alive!
description: Caryocorbula contracta is a small, wedge-shaped clam that lives buried in muddy ocean bottoms along New England's coast. These tiny mollusks typically measure less than half an inch across, with two unequal shell halves that fit together like puzzle pieces. The shells are usually whitish to pale yellow with a somewhat chalky appearance. They're part of a group called corbulid clams, which are known for their distinctive asymmetrical shells.

idTips.label: Shell asymmetry
idTips.description: The two shell halves are noticeably different sizes - one valve is larger and overlaps the smaller one like a lid on a box, creating an uneven, lopsided appearance

idTips.label: Wedge shape
idTips.description: The shell forms a distinctive triangular or wedge profile when viewed from the side, tapering from a rounded front to a pointed rear end

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Tiny shells rarely exceed 12mm (about half an inch) in length, small enough to fit comfortably on your thumbnail

idTips.label: Surface texture
idTips.description: Shells feel smooth to slightly chalky with fine growth lines that you can barely feel when running your finger across the surface

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Usually dull white to pale yellowish, sometimes with a slightly translucent quality when held up to light

habitat: These small clams live buried in soft, muddy sediments in shallow coastal waters and estuaries along New England's shores. They prefer areas with fine mud or sandy mud bottoms where they can easily burrow, typically in depths from the low tide zone down to about 100 feet. You're most likely to find empty shells washed up on mudflat beaches after storms.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells may wash ashore after winter storms. Living clams are actively feeding in the warming sediments.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period for living clams buried in the mud. Empty shells are less commonly found on beaches during calmer weather.
seasonality.fall: Autumn storms begin to expose more shells on beaches as wave action increases and disturbs bottom sediments.
seasonality.winter: Storm-tossed shells are most commonly found on beaches after nor'easters churn up the sea bottom.

funFact: Despite being less than half an inch long, these tiny clams can live for over 10 years buried in the mud, filtering microscopic food from seawater while staying in the same small burrow their entire lives!
confusionNotes: The asymmetrical shells easily distinguish these from common symmetrical clams like quahogs or steamers. Remember: if the two shell halves look obviously different sizes and one overlaps the other like a tiny hinged box, you've likely found a corbulid clam.
contextualKnowledge: This species is uncommon in New England waters and represents the northern edge of its range - it's much more abundant in warmer southern waters, making any New England finds particularly noteworthy for shell collectors.
compareHints: Since this is the only Caryocorbula species commonly found in New England waters, compare it with other small clams in the corbulid family. Unlike more symmetrical small clams such as gem clams or coquinas, Caryocorbula contracta's most distinctive feature is always the unequal shell valves where one clearly overlaps and is larger than the other. This asymmetry is the key family trait that separates all corbulid clams from their relatives.
